concept: Lucene BBQ binary quantization compared with Atlas binary quantization
summary: Source-anchored research for Lucene BBQ binary quantization compared with Atlas binary quantization. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Elastic documents BBQ as compressing each vector by 32x (float32 to bits) plus 14 bytes of corrective data per vector, and lists bbq_hnsw as about 32x less memory. MongoDB documents 32x smaller vector values for binary quantization but only about 24x less mongot RAM, because the HNSW graph itself doesn't shrink. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md ; https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/bbq

RaBitQ supplies the research lineage and a theoretical error bound. Elastic's BBQ announcement lists differences from the original RaBitQ implementation, including no random rotation of the codebook (so the estimator is not unbiased over multiple invocations) and rescoring not being done during graph index search. The RaBitQ guarantee should not automatically be attributed to BBQ. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12497 ; https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/better-binary-quantization-lucene-elasticsearch

BBQ uses asymmetric scoring: stored document coordinates use one bit, while query coordinates use four bits. This differs from the binary query conversion described for Atlas. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/better-binary-quantization-lucene-elasticsearch ; https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/elasticsearch-bbq-osq-vs-turbo ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md

BBQ evolved beyond its launch implementation: Elastic describes per-vector optimized quantization intervals, centroid centering and stored correction terms in its OSQ-backed implementation. Comparisons should identify the Elasticsearch/Lucene version rather than assuming earlier implementations are unchanged. (high confidence)

OpenSearch issue 2805 reports recall@100 of 0.32 versus 0.18 on SIFT-128 and 0.63 versus 0.30 on Cohere-768-1M for Lucene BBQ versus Faiss binary quantization without oversampling. This is an implementation-specific benchmark against Faiss, not evidence that BBQ outperforms Atlas. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-25)

Recall recovery depends on data and candidate depth. Elastic advises that higher compression generally needs more oversampling to recover recall, and that no single oversample value fits every model and dataset, so recall and latency should be measured on your own data. Sources: https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/vector/knn/optimize-performance-accuracy

VectorDBBench documents Elastic Cloud HNSW_BBQ runs with candidate-count controls and exposes rescoring and oversampling options. It offers a reproducible harness starting point, but its README alone does not constitute a controlled Atlas-versus-BBQ result. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas automatic binary quantization is documented as mapping each original coordinate above zero to 1 and all others to 0, with the query converted using the same midpoint. BBQ instead centers vectors around a segment centroid and uses correction metadata; the binary-quantization label does not establish algorithmic equivalence. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md ; https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/better-binary-quantization-lucene-elasticsearch

Both systems retain original vectors on disk for rescoring. Atlas stores full fidelity vectors on disk and references them only during rescoring; Elasticsearch keeps the original vectors on disk for rescoring, which increases disk use. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/about/vector-quantization.md ; https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/vector/knn/optimize-performance-accuracy

Evaluate vector-search recall and latency alongside candidate exploration (num_candidates) and rescoring with the original vectors. Quantization reduces RAM but costs some recall, and the original vectors stay on disk for rescoring. Sources: https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/vector/knn/optimize-performance-accuracy
